blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: Thank you, my Lord. Dr Bohin, welcome back.
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: I forgot to ask about one thing yesterday before I move on to the issue of what happened in Arrowe Park before [Baby G] was transferred into the Countess of Chester for the first time. I just want to deal with this one issue first and show you a photograph that you have seen before and you were asked to comment on in the witness statement that you made on 7 April 2022.
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: It's in your comments/opinion section, which, if your print is the same as I have, is the bottom of page 2.
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: What would you say from your experience about this photograph?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Well, it shows that [Baby G] was nursed in that particular type of bed, a Kanbed, which has very high sides and what the photograph shows is that the position of the vomit would have meant that she would have had to have exerted a huge amount of force to have vomited -- from being on her back to have vomited over the side of the cot and on to the floor and also even further, several feet, on to the chair.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: I just find that surprising, given that she was only 2 kilograms at that time, that she could generate enough force to make vomit travel that sort of distance. So you know, clearly that's what happened and that seems extraordinary to me.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: How many years' experience do you have of dealing with children of this sort of age?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: My first neonatal job was in 1986, so over 30 years.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: Yes, 36 years. Have you ever encountered a situation in which a child that doesn't have the pyloric stenosis condition that we heard about yesterday has vomited like that?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: No.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: Have you ever heard of a case in which a child who didn't have pyloric stenosis vomited to that extent?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: No. I mean, you know, it's very common for babies to vomit and certainly in older children with gastroenteritis they vomit quite forcefully, as anyone who's had a child will know. But they are usually sitting up -- because they're older children, they're usually sitting up when they vomit, and they are much bigger than 2 kilograms, which is what -- [Baby G]'s weight was only 2 kilograms and I have never seen a baby of that size forcefully vomit or projectile vomit in that way to that extent.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: Yesterday at the close of business, the jury asked a question. I'll read it to you and ask whether you can answer it, please.
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: The question is this:
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: "What is the maximum amount of fluid a baby of [Baby G]'s size's stomach could hold? How much would cause the diaphragm to be compromised?"
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: This may be two questions, so shall I deal with each individually?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: "What's the maximum amount of fluid a baby of [Baby G]'s size's stomach could hold?"
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: That's an excellent question and something that I've looked into myself. Unfortunately, there isn't a right answer. There's nothing much in the literature to enlighten us on that. People have looked at the volume of a stomach in a term baby who was not being fed, so has never had anything in the stomach, and that is very small. And what happens over time in term babies is that as the feeds increase day on day, the stomach, which is muscular, stretches to be able to accommodate that. But there's no research that I could find that would allow me to inform the jury of the volume of a stomach.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: What I know from my own experience, and being at post-mortems, the neonatal stomach in a 2-kilogram baby is very small, about the size of a plum, but it can actually extend a lot. And in a baby who's been fed over many weeks and months, as [Baby G] was, the stomach would actually have enlarged. So it's absolutely impossible to be precise and tell the jury the volume of a stomach in a baby who had been fed for many months.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: Yes. And the second part or the second question?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: "How much would cause the diaphragm to be compromised?"
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Is there an answer to that?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Again, that's impossible to say because for some babies with normal lungs, a distended tummy might press up on to their lungs only a small amount and wouldn't actually affect very much. But in [Baby G]'s case we know that her lungs were not normal because she had chronic lung disease and so most probably there wouldn't need to be much distension before her lungs were compromised. But in terms of the volume in the stomach, I'm afraid I can't give an answer to that.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: Thank you very much.
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Sorry, could I just say that I should have mentioned to the jury that I received that note from one of you; I don't know whether you discussed it between yourselves. After we rose yesterday afternoon I handed it to counsel and it was going to be dealt with today.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: But you have heard the doctor's answer to it, that's as far as it can be taken, thank you, with this witness certainly. I don't know whether any other witnesses will be able to assist or not.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: Well, I doubt it, but...
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: So do I, but...
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: Dr Bohin, can I move on, please, to a witness statement that you made on -- not very long ago, actually, about 3 weeks ago, on 23 November 2022.
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: Is it right that you were asked to look at whether there was any clinical evidence that [Baby G] was intolerant of feeds at any point whilst she was an inpatient at either Arrowe Park Hospital or the Countess of Chester Hospital?
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: You were asked to comment on whether vomiting was a notable clinical feature whilst [Baby G] was an inpatient at either Arrowe Park or the Countess of Chester.
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: And thirdly, you were asked to look at the issue of whether there was any clinical evidence to support the diagnosis of gastro-oesophageal reflux in [Baby G].
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Yes, that's correct.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: Did that cause you to go, in effect, back to the beginning, so far as [Baby G] was concerned, to the time of her birth at the end of May 2015?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Yes, it did. I needed to read very thoroughly the nursing and medical and observation charts for the whole of her feeding history.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: So taking things up at your paragraph 2.3 then, please, did you observe what we have established in evidence, namely that [Baby G] was born on 31 May 2015?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: And that enteral feeds, so milk feeds, were cautiously commenced at half of 1 millilitre every 4 hours via a nasogastric tube on 15 June 2015?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: Merely summarising the position, were those feeds tolerated and gradually increased?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Yes, they were.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: And full feeds of milk were reached by 22 June 2015?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: And as always, are full feeds calculated on the basis of so much in millilitres per kilo per day?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: And in [Baby G]'s case was that 150ml per kilo per day?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: At that stage, yes.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: Yes. I know this wasn't the position, but if she had been still about half a kilo in weight, she would have received 75ml per kilo per day?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: At that point?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: Putting that into context, that would be roughly, in very rough terms, about just under 3 millilitres an hour over a 24-hour period --
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: -- give or take?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: Was she actually fed initially hourly via the nasogastric tube?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Yes, she was fed hourly for a long time.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: Yes, and was there any vomiting or nasogastric aspirates, and if so, to what extent in Arrowe Park?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: There was no vomiting and the nursing staff recorded the nasogastric aspirates as minimal, which I take to be less than a millilitre really.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: Because feeds, the breast milk, was tolerated, was some fortifier added from 26 June 2015?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Yes. I think it's probably around that time there was a plan to add fortifier a day or so before. Fortifier is usually added as half strength first of all and then if that's tolerated goes up to full strength. So the notes aren't really clear about
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: when she went to full strength fortifier, but it was around -she was definitely receiving it on the 26th.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: Was there a hiatus in feeding breast milk because [Baby G] had to have this Broviac line inserted by the surgeons at Alder Hey Hospital in Liverpool on 26 June?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Yes. She'd had a pulmonary haemorrhage and required a Broviac line and the Broviac line is inserted under general anaesthetic and so feeds would have needed to be stopped, but they were reintroduced -- within the same day.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: Yes. So thereafter, can you take us through [Baby G]'s feeding history by reference to paragraph 2.6 of your report, please?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Yes. The feeds on 30 June were hourly feeds and they were running at 3ml every hour. The decision was made to increase that volume to 4ml every hour. When that happened, [Baby G] had a single large nasogastric aspirate.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: The volume wasn't recorded, it just says "large aspirate".
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: The medical team were informed, they decided not to stop the feeds, the feeds were continued, and thereafter were well tolerated to the extent that breast milk fortifier was reintroduced later on that day.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: Would you like me to continue?
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: Yes, please. So that's 30 June. Did you then move on to a change on 3 July?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Yes. Between 30th and the 3rd, [Baby G] continued to feed on hourly nasogastric feeds. On 3 July, the feeds were increased from 150ml per kilogram of body weight per day to 165ml per kilogram of body weight per day. This was because she hadn't been gaining weight that well and in light of that the volume given was increased in an attempt to get her to gain weight.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: That increase was well tolerated and there was no vomiting or increased nasogastric aspirates. What the staff did note -- that [Baby G] had developed frequent desaturations, but these were self-correcting, which means that she very briefly desaturated but managed to get her saturations up without any help or intervention from nursing staff.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: Thank you.
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: There's a nursing entry that mentions introducing antireflux medication for the desaturations and that was the first
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: mention of gastro-oesophageal reflux that I could find in the notes. And coincidentally, with these desaturations and the mention of anti-reflux medication, [Baby G] developed very thick secretions from her breathing, her endotracheal breathing tube, and these did subsequently grow a bug.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: Is that also on 3 July?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Yes. On 3 July there was also a ward round note, so as well as the nurses saying that there should be -- that the antireflux medication should be optimised, there's a ward round note on that day, again saying that there was a plan to optimise management of reflux, but reflux had not been mentioned prior to that at all. But what they did was they elevated the cot a little bit. So the standard practice is to elevate the head end of the cot by about 30 degrees so that, just by pure physics and gravity, it's very difficult or more difficult to vomit if you're sitting up or you're elevated.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: They also started a course of erythromycin, which is an antibiotic. It's not really clear why they started that. There are two possible reasons. One is that erythromycin can act as a prokinetic, so it can act as a way of advancing your stomach contents through the stomach, so that's one reason. But also in the notes it mentions covering for an organism called ureaplasma, which is a rare organism found in babies with chronic lung disease and erythromycin is also the treatment for that and the notes don't make it clear whether erythromycin was prescribed as a prokinetic to help the reflux or to help with ureaplasma.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: They also decided to start a medication called Gaviscon which adults can use as well as babies. In babies it comes as a powder that you can add to the milk. It makes the milk slightly thicker if given in large doses, but in the kind of dose that they were giving to [Baby G] there would not have been any obvious noticeable difference.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: But what Gaviscon does, when it's in the stomach, it kinds of forms a sort of raft over the top of the stomach contents and it makes it more difficult for you to vomit them.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: Yes. I think there's an image of that on the TV adverts for Gaviscon.
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Possibly! It's not clear from the notes when Gaviscon was started and there's no reference to starting Gaviscon in the medical notes, but there is reference in the nursing notes and there is a prescription that I can find when Gaviscon was actually given.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: Thereafter, how did [Baby G] progress? I'm moving on to your paragraph 2.9.
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Yes. [Baby G] improved. She was extubated on to BiPAP, so a kind of fancy form of CPAP really, on 7 July. She continued to tolerate feeds, which by this time were 5ml every hour.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: On 12 July, the feeds were increased again to 180ml per kilogram per day. Previously they'd been 165ml per kilogram per day, so they were increased to 180 and then to 190ml per kilo per day on the 15th. So the volume she was receiving had increased because her weight gain was still sub-optimal and the team were trying to maximise her weight gain. But this change in feed volume was well tolerated, it wasn't associated with any vomiting or large aspirates.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: Thank you. Moving on to 31 July.
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Yes. On 31st, [Baby G] had three desaturations which were not self-correcting and required a brief increase in her oxygen concentration. But thereafter, she recovered, she continued to have very fleeting self-correcting desaturations after feeds, which is very normal in neonates of this size.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: She had a single large nasogastric aspirate of 10ml prior to the feed at 5 o'clock and that feed was subsequently omitted but then she was fed thereafter without any problems so there was just one single large aspirate of 10ml.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: That was still the 31st?
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: That was on the 31st, yes. She remained well and it is of note that on 1/8, she was given her immunisations and that -you just would not give immunisations if a baby was unwell. So she must have been well and stable for the team to have considered giving her her immunisations on that day.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: Does that follow as a general principle that if the medics are actively considering giving immunisations to a child of this age then the view must be that the child is well?
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: Yes, because immunisations can upset babies and can just destabilise them, so you wouldn't consider giving immunisations unless a baby was absolutely stable.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: And we know that immunisations were being considered on the 6th and 7 September when [Baby G] had her incident that we have been exploring for the last few days in evidence.
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: That's correct.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: So that would be a reflection of the view that had been taken medically of her before the desaturation?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: Moving on to 3 August then, please.
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Yes. On 3 August [Baby G] had an increase in her desaturations and also these were accompanied by bradycardias, so a slowing of her heart rate. In view of that, the medical team were cautious and did an infection screen and started her on antibiotics.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: Feeds, however, were continued and she continued to tolerate feeds, which were still running at 190ml per kilogram per day. There was no vomiting and aspirates were minimal. So although it was the right thing to do to cover for infection, the feeds continued without a problem.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: On 12 August, [Baby G] was well, was doing so well that the feeds were increased to two-hourly from hourly, and that change in -- so that means then that she was given double the amount but on alternate hours as opposed to hourly and that change was well tolerated.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: Yes. And what does the fact that the feeds were doubled but the incidence of the feeds were halved, so to speak, or doubled mean?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: That means [Baby G] could tolerate that sort of doubling of volume in her stomach and that her stomach could accommodate that.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: Yes. So following that increase of the quantity being given because the frequency was halved -- or doubled as well, I should say --
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: -- was [Baby G] then transferred from Arrowe Park on the Wirral to the Countess of Chester Hospital on 13 August?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: So far as the discharge summary was concerned, first of all can you tell us what a discharge summary is and then tell us what it said so far as [Baby G] and her ability to tolerate feeds was concerned?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Yes. All neonatal units in the UK have a computerised neonatal discharge summary that is electronic, that is shared
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: between neonatal units, so that information can be shared between the units and this was the case with [Baby G]. It's usually the job of the most junior person in the department to write the discharge summary. It's called Badger because that's the name of the man who developed the system. On the Badger summary it's usually the SHO who does that and clearly this person had their work cut out because [Baby G] had had a very difficult time when she was at Arrowe Park. She had a very long period of intensive care with lots of problems, so it would have been difficult. That first episode has probably got almost 2,000 pages of notes for the SHO to have gone through.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: What they tend to do for the GP and the hospital that the baby is being transferred to is write a list of the main problems that the baby's suffered during their stay, and then, system by system, go through it, so they would write a paragraph on the respiratory system and the problems that ensued, write a next list of problems with the heart, problems with feeding, problems with neurology, how many bloods transfusions you've had, how many infection screens you've had, all of those details are the -- the whole episode is kind of précised into one summary.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: Finally, for the accepting hospital they would usually give the current status of the baby, the current weight, what the feeding regime is, the current problems that the receiving hospital need to be aware of, and a list of medication.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: In [Baby G]'s summary there was no mention of the fact that she was on Gaviscon and no mention that gastro-oesophageal reflux was being seen as a potential problem for her.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: Did the Countess of Chester notes mention gastrooesophageal reflux?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Yes. In their very first medical entry -- I think it was Dr Ventress -- she's written in their problem list that gastrooesophageal reflux was a potential problem.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: So although it wasn't in the discharge letter, I would imagine she had had a verbal correspondence with the people at Arrowe Park because that would be normal for you to have a verbal handover as well as having a very detailed discharge letter, but it's mentioned in their list.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: We haven't given the jury the feeding charts going back to 13 August, but you have reviewed them. What do they show so far as [Baby G]'s ability to tolerate two-hourly feeds between her transfer into Chester on 13 August and the events about which the jury have been hearing evidence, which occurred in the early hours of 7 September?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: The feeding charts show that the feeds were well tolerated with no vomits, no large aspirates. The nursing notes mention the occasional self-correcting bradycardia, so a drop in heart rate, after feeds. They were noted but [Baby G] didn't become unwell or destabilised, and that is so common as to almost be a normal feature in neonates.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: On 24 August, so about 2 weeks before 7 September, was [Baby G] put onto three-hourly feeds, so upped from two-hourly to three-hourly feeds?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: Did somebody by mistake give her 45ml of feed instead of 36ml?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Yes. The three-hourly amount was 36ml, which she had been tolerating, but in error at 8.45 she was given 45ml by mistake. But despite this increase in volume, she tolerated that, there was no vomiting and it was well tolerated.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: So this is an increase of 9ml on a feed that should have been 36ml?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: Sorry, just the date and time of that.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: 8.45 on the 24th.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: Yes, 08.45 am.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: So it's an increase of exactly 25%, isn't it?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: An accidental increase of 25% results in no problems for [Baby G]?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Correct.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: Thank you. Did those three-hourly feeds continue?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Yes, she went back to three-hourly feeds with the added Gaviscon.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: And were there any issues so far as aspirates or vomiting were concerned?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: No vomiting and the aspirates were said to be minimal by the nursing staff.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: Did the issue of self-correcting desaturations continue?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Yes, they were noted during and after feeds.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: But did they cause a problem?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: No.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: And so bringing us up to date so far as [Baby G]'s collapse is concerned and going back to divider 7 in the bundle that the jury has, the number 2 bundle, going to the back of that bundle to find the feeding charts, it's the penultimate change, the one before the end, J7012. Did you look at those?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: And what conclusions or observations did you make?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: It's clear that, certainly by the 6th, [Baby G] was receiving alternate tube and -- nasogastric tube and bottle feeds. They were three-hourly feeds. They were tolerated. There was no vomiting, there's no mention of aspirates, and where the nasogastric tube has been tested for acidity, certainly on the 5th, the nurses just marked "positive for acid" without actually writing down a pH. But at 20.00 on the 6th, the nurse has written that there is a pH of 4, which is obviously acid, and that's before the nasogastric feed, but all those feeds are well tolerated.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: Yes. Is that acidic -- we know that's [Nurse E], she told us that was her signature. Is that pH value of 4, so an acidic value, consistent with there being a large amount of undigested milk in the stomach?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: No, it's not. Milk is neutral and gastric contents are acid. A pH of 4 is very acidic. If there was undigested milk or milk in the stomach, that would buffer or neutralise the pH and you would expect the pH to be higher than that.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: So a neutral -- I'm sure the jury all know this, but a neutral substance, be it milk, be it water, added to an acidic substance reduces the level of acidity?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Yes. So a neutral pH is 7. Anything less than that is slightly acidic. I have reviewed the subsequent feeding charts from Arrowe Park and indeed the Countess of Chester and where there have been minimal aspirates or where there have been milky
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: aspirates, the pH is usually around 5.5 or 5, but never gets as low as 4, where there are milky aspirates obtained.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: Yes. And thus, turning the page in the jury bundle to [Nurse E]'s entry at 02.00 hours on 7 September, what conclusions do you draw from your expertise as to whether or not [Baby G] had a large volume of undigested milk in her stomach when [Nurse E] put in 45ml?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: In my opinion, the stomach was empty at that time because the pH is 4 and I wouldn't expect the pH to be that low if there was a large volume of undigested milk in the stomach.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: And thus, as a consequence of her having vomited in a projectile way, as we have heard described, and there then having been recovered or aspirated from her stomach the 45ml of feed, what conclusions do you draw as to what was in her stomach and what caused her to vomit?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: She must have had an additional volume of milk in her stomach because there's no way that -- she had an empty stomach here at 02.00, she was then fed, and so she must at some point after that feed have been given an excessive amount of milk in order for her to be able to projectile vomit a huge amount and have a 45ml residual within her stomach.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: Is there anything in the records to reasonably suggest that prior to this incident she was a child that was prone to vomiting?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: No.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: Thank you, Dr Bohin. Would you wait there, please?
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: Cross-examination by MR MYERS
I'm making a note of one thing before I commence, my Lord.
blocks.speaker: MR MYERS

blocks.text: Yes, certainly.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: (Pause)

blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: So the fact that she desaturated then, you cannot establish that that was down to her being fed, it was down to the fact that she was seriously ill, and I think she probably was also on nitric oxide at that time which is, yes, a further step forward. blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: Just so it's clear, I'm not going through this to try to link this to feeding. So we can all follow, this is to look at how unwell [Baby G] was.

blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: You still have a tube, but it's a different machine, a different mechanism. It's used for the sickest and most vulnerable babies, as is inhaled nitric oxide, which she also received.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: Sorry, Mr Myers.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: Not at all, my Lord.
blocks.speaker: MR MYERS

blocks.text: The next page I would like to go to, please, is page 4216, and we're moving forward to 4 June.
blocks.speaker: MR MYERS

blocks.text: These are notes for 4 June and the entry I'm going to go to is for 23.45 on 4 June. Thank you.
blocks.speaker: MR MYERS

blocks.text: 23.45. It says:
blocks.speaker: MR MYERS

blocks.text: "Written retrospectively."
blocks.speaker: MR MYERS

blocks.text: These are, of course, clinical notes, and over the page we have the signature of the doctor who signed off, but it's just the starting part that I'm going to.

blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: "... desaturating down to 60s. Good chest wobble.

blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: Thank you. In fact, I'm just going to go to the top of the page if I could as well. That note that we've just looked at deals with the situation from 22.30. This is a note at 23.00, so just beforehand, and how [Baby G] presented at 22.15:

blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: "Good wobble seen. Abdo looks distended."
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Um...
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: (Pause)
Or if it isn't, please say.
blocks.speaker: MYERS

That sort of ventilation with the nitric oxide is about as much ventilation as you could possibly give to a baby. So she was as sick as you could possibly be and therefore it would not be uncommon to have desaturations or
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: bradycardias or whatever. If you're that sick, that's kind of normal for a baby in intensive care who is that unwell.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: Right, thank you.

blocks.text: Yes.

blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: (overspeaking) and they've had the result and then you say that there's the issue with the chin.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: So it's clearly linked in time and they are linked as a sequence. They appear to be two --
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: It does appear to be two, you are absolutely correct, because this mentions the chin on the chest, yes.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: Thank you. It's my fault for going back to front with that. I apologise. I'm grateful.
blocks.speaker: MR MYERS

blocks.text: Let's move forwards to 6 June, please. That's page 4227. As is quite apparent from what I've dealt with already, Dr Bohin, we are moving forwards over very large numbers of medical notes. These are just examples. These are clinical notes by the doctor who's treating and we're just looking at the top half of the page, please, looking at some of the features we find.
blocks.speaker: MR MYERS

blocks.text: It's an entry for 01.30. Not the easiest writing to decipher but that's not unique in this case. It says:
blocks.speaker: MR MYERS

blocks.text: "Cannula..."
blocks.speaker: MR MYERS

blocks.text: Is that "thought to be"?
blocks.speaker: MR MYERS

blocks.text: "... thought to be leaking by nursing staff."
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: "Sodium bicarbonate infusions stopped."
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: "Following gas and some..."?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: "Handling."
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: Handling.
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: "... saturations dropped..."
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: "... to the low 60s."
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: It then -- let's read through this note. It's relatively short:
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: "If FOV MAP..."
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Can you hep us with that, please?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: HFOV is high frequency oscillation ventilation, which is the oscillation I spoke about:
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: "Mean airway pressure [is MAP] increased to 10.5 but no improvement in oxygenation."
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: I can't read the next thing and:
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: "Mean blood pressure dropped to 37 from 40."
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: I think it's "noted".
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: Oh yes, "noted".
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.speaker: MR MYERS

blocks.text: "MAP returned to 10 and adrenaline increased to 2 micrograms per kilogram per minute."
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: So [Baby G] was on an adrenaline infusion for her blood pressure, which shows me -- that's not the first line medication for blood pressure so that shows me that her blood pressure was clearly a problem. Then it goes on to talk about the examination.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: It says:
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: "Oedematous, good wobble. Abdo soft but discoloured."
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: That's what it has recorded on this occasion, isn't it?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Soft but discoloured and she was paralysed as well so (inaudible) paralysis.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: Right. And Dr Rackham -- "Discussed with Dr Rackham on the phone"?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: "Maximise inotropes to optimise perfusion."
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: So again increase the adrenaline or add another inotrope:
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: "Try brief suction of the endotracheal tube.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: Minimise handling. Not for re-cannulation at present."
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: Thank you.
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: So she didn't tolerate any sort of handling and would immediately drop her saturations and her oxygenation, so they wanted to minimise that, but then there's the conundrum because she needed a new drip, so that means that you need a lot of handling.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: We see from that again a propensity for her oxygen saturation to drop, which it does on handling on this occasion, doesn't it?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: It does in the early stages of her life, in the beginning, of June, yes. That's in the first week or so of her life when she was gravely ill.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: We'll carry on. Also we notice the abdomen is discoloured.
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: The abdomen is discoloured there, but this is a baby who's only 500-odd grams and so would have no subcutaneous fat at all and therefore the abdomen in babies that are that small often looks discoloured because you can see the blood vessels in the skin and you can see the bowel and the bowel almost through the skin as the skin is almost translucent. That doesn't necessarily mean that there's pathology there, that's quite normal in a baby that's that tiny.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: Thank you. Can we move, please, next to page 4461, which is later the same day, and this is in the nursing notes. Which you are going to see, it has to be said, it might be thought by some, are an awful lot easier to read than the Countess of Chester nursing notes.
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: This is a nursing note at Arrowe Park Hospital.
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: We can see it relates to [Baby G] and it has her date of birth. It has the name of the nurse on the right-hand side where it says "electronically signed by", or at least I take that to be the name of the nurse, and it has a date and time so we can see when the entry is made, and this is at 20.32 on 6 June. The last entry was at 1.30 that morning. We can see it relates to [Baby G] and it says in the body of the text:
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: "Head scan done this afternoon. Abdominal X-ray done as abdomen shiny and some distension and some colour change. Plan to commence on metronidazole.
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Insulin recommenced this evening."
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Then reference to other medication, but I just identify there:
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: "Abdominal X-ray done as abdomen shiny. Some distension and some colour change."
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Was she -- did you recall whether at this point she was on any type of feed or is it all intravenous at this stage?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: It was all intravenous. She didn't start her feeds until the inotropes, which are drugs to help your blood pressure, until they were stopped because if you feed a baby then in order to digest it you have to divert blood to the gut in order to help/aid with digestion and clearly they didn't want to do that while she was so gravely ill and on lots of drugs to help her blood pressure. And also in a baby that has problems with low blood pressure if you feed them you will increase their risk of developing necrotising enterocolitis, which is clearly what they were concerned about there because they did the X-ray and then they added in metronidazole to her antibiotic regimen, which would be normal practice, to be very, very cautious in a baby
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: that was so gravely ill in case she was developing necrotising enterocolitis.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: So far as we know she didn't develop necrotising enterocolitis?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: No, she didn't, but it was still the correct thing to add in the metronidazole.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: Of course. So the distension would be due it a build-up of gas unrelated to the feeds; is that right?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: And some clear change but, as you've explained, seeing colour change in the abdomen of a very small child is something you might expect to find?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Well, you would always find that in a baby of only 500odd grams, yes.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: Next, please, the following day, 7 June 2015, page 4238.
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: It's an entry we can see at the top half of the page so if we enlarge that part, please. 7 June 2015, 6.30 in the morning. It's the first part I'm interested in going to, but we have the rest of it to see:
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: "Attended to patient as desaturation to 60s. No bradycardia at 05.35. Over 15-minute period repeatedly dropping sats to mid- 60s/70s. Improving with Neopuffing but then dropping again. Occurred after change in baby's position. Good AE bilaterally on auscultation."
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: In other words that's listening, is that, and AE is that air entry?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: "Good chest wall movement. Cold light applied."
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Is that to see if there's any damage or any pneumothorax?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: It is to see if there's any pneumothorax.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: It says -- is that:
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: "Increased transillumination on the right side"?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: "Oxygen gradually increased to 100% but sats sitting in low 80s. Rate goes back to 55 flow 50 [as read]."
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: "From 50."
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: Sorry, my fault:
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: "... from 50. Called Dr Hughes who attended within 50 minutes. Urgent X-ray performed."
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: And the X-ray is then reviewed:
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: "No pneumothorax, no significant change previously."
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: Again, just identifying there, recognising this is only just after we're about a week old with [Baby G] now, but again a propensity to desaturate. She's very young, very unwell, but she is desaturating repeatedly at this point, isn't she?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes, I think the distinction needs to be made between the desaturations in a critically ill baby who is receiving this amount of intensive care to a baby that is several months old who is not receiving that amount of intensive care and the causes are different -- the causes of the desaturations are different.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: All right, thank you. We'll move forward a week then to 14 June. Page 4271, please.
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: These are notes on 14 June at 08.00. We can see a review setting out medication at the top of the page.
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: If we scroll down the page it says:
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: "Sepsis."
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Underlined?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: That just is trying to state the position with -- for anybody else who reads the notes where we are in terms of sepsis because it's so common in babies who are this sick.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: All right. where I'd like to go to is down to where it says "on examination". So apologies, Mr Murphy, for coming out of that. But "on examination", just to see what is said there.
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: "Pale pink. Capillary refill time less than 2 seconds.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: AF [anterior fontanelle] soft. Some oedema [which is swelling] persists. Desaturated on handling to the 80s [which is completely normal in a baby which is this sick]. (inaudible) squeaky bilateral air entry. CDS.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: Both heart sounds present with no added sounds. GIT [gut]/abdo not examined as prone."
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: So that meant that she was being nursed on her tummy.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: All right. What I'm identifying there is that desaturations on handling continue but, as you identify, she's still very young and receiving a lot of support?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: It would be normal for a baby that ill to desaturate whenever she was touched, which is actually why we have minimal handling of these babies. So they are only touched when absolutely necessary because of that very fact that they tend to desaturate.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: Thank you. Next, the same day -- that was at 08.00 and the next entry is for 23.38 that evening, and it's in the nursing notes at page 4510, please, Mr Murphy.
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: It's easy to enlarge the top part of that page.
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: This is -- we see -- I'm going to straight to the time and the date first, 14 June, 23.38. We have the name of the nurse. Just underneath there we have the progress note. I'm going to go to that:
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: "[Baby G] is now 14 days old and stable, therefore incubator changed and came out for first cuddles.
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Tolerated cuddles well and settled back in incubator.
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Saturating well but last blood gas poor, therefore rate increased and suction..."
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: It says "suction 7 given", but it should be "suction given" maybe?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: "Minimal secretions from ET: small, bloodstained."
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Do you see that?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: Nothing remarkable about ET tube being small and bloodstained in this situation, is there?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: No. Because I would imagine she would have been having fairly regular suction of that ET tube in order to keep it patent.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: Yes, but it is entirely possible to get secretions, small, bloodstained, around the ET tube without there being any deliberate harm, isn't it?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Well, the nursing staff would have been causing trauma by putting the suction catheter through an ET tube, so if you get bloodstained secretions because you have been suctioning down the ET tube, that is a consequence of the nurses doing cares and ensuring that that tube is patent. That's very different to having bloodstained secretions where there's no ET tube present.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: So an ET tube in itself, if there's been suction taking place, could cause bloodstained secretions; is that right?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: It can do depending on how aggressive, I guess, the nurse is being, but also what I don't know is at this time were things like her platelets normal because if her platelets were low -on the previous note that you showed me her platelets were only 22, so if her platelets were low then any sort of intervention like that would cause bleeding.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: In fact she had a transfusion -- I don't know if we have page 4818 available, but she was given a transfusion at 13.55 that day.
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Of platelets or blood?
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: Of blood -- platelet transfusion. I wonder if it's possible to put up page 4818 so we can confirm this. It isn't on the list, Mr Murphy, but if it's possible.
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: I don't have it here.
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: If we just look at the top. Can you see 14 June, the low entry?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: "Platelets, 11ml."
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes. So she had low platelets on that day and they treated her with a platelet transfusion. So prior to receiving those platelets, her platelets would have been low enough that any sort of intervention would have caused bleeding.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: Yes. Just to be clear, you didn't know whether there had been a transfusion or what her platelets were?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: No.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: Taking that, first of all. At 1.55, so about 10 hours before this, 9.5 hours, she had been given a platelet transfusion, hadn't she?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: Right. Thank you. That's done to assist with clotting, isn't it?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: It is and it's often given because the baby's got an infection and the infection is consuming their platelets so the fact that she was given platelets then doesn't tell me what her platelet count was at the time the suction was carried out because it may well have dropped again.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: But you asked, so I was just establishing (overspeaking) done.
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes, thank you very much.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: Let's move forward, please, then to 17 June, which is at page 4282. This is a note that goes over two pages.
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: The first page, let's have a look, and it's the bottom part of the page. Thank you:
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: "17/6/15. 12.30. Written in retrospect. ST4 Callaghan. Called into the room. Desat to 40s and previous episode of bradycardia. Desat improved slowly with Neopuff but sats still in 60s. ET tube removed.

blocks.text: Perhaps we can just see what's over the page before I come back to that. I don't know if we're able to go to the page that follows. Thank you, Mr Murphy.

blocks.text: "Two attempts at intubation by ANNP Collins."

blocks.text: sedation at that stage, although I can't confirm that, but it would be unusual for her not to be.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: Even in those circumstances, and small as she was, it appeared that the tube moved position even after it had first been put into her; is that correct?

blocks.text: With these attempts or the previous one? The previous tube was removed because she was desaturating and they removed the tube and there was a clot at the end of it, so she needed to be re-intubated, and it looks like the first doctor tried and was unsuccessful. The second doctor tried and the tube was dislodged. The second doctor tried again, was successful, but then subsequently the tube slipped in a bit further than it should have done and these tubes are, in this case, only 2.5 millimetres wide, and they go into the trachea and then they're secured at the lips and they're secured by a clamp, which should stop it moving backwards and forwards, because it would be easy to come out but if it goes in too it far it tends to go down into the right lung preferentially, just because of how the anatomy is.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: And if that happens, when you listen to the chest, rather than hearing air entry the same on both sides, you hear loud air entry on the right and reduced air entry on the left, which is what that doctor describes, because the tube had slipped down too far.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: Once they pulled it back -- it had gone down to 5 centimetres at the lips, so once they pulled it back the air entry was equal again. So that would cause a baby to destabilise because you're then only ventilating one lung.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: What we're looking at on that page shows one incidence where the tube it had dislodged and another when it had slipped in; is that right?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yet.

blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Well, not really, because this baby's likely to have been (a) sedated and on the previous air entry -- on the previous things we looked at the baby was actually paralysed, so I'm not sure on this occasion whether the baby's on sedation or paralysed, because if she were then there would be -- if people had secured the tube correctly with the clamp there would be no reason for the tube to move in because it should be fixed and firm as the baby's not moving about to dislodge it herself.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: But what we do see is, whatever's happened, there is movement of the tube in that baby even when sedated, isn't there?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: It appears so, yes.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: All right.
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Just before we leave that, you said these tubes are 2.5 millimetres.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: Wide.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: Wide:
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: "Second attempt, successful. 2.5 centimetres ET tube."

blocks.text: Ah.

blocks.speaker: MR MYERS

blocks.text: It just didn't make sense when that was being read and when I heard the doctor say 2.5 millimetres I realised
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: Absolutely. That's what I wanted to ask about the tubes and movement of the tubes. Can we just go back then to the beginning of the note and let me just return to that. So back to the page before, Mr Murphy, if you would, please.
blocks.speaker: MR MYERS

blocks.text: Just that note that we have there. Again another instance of [Baby G] desaturating, correct, Dr Bohin?

blocks.text: When the ET tube was removed a clot and secretions on the end of the ET tube, isn't it, which is -- that's something you might expect to find on an ET tube once a baby has been intubated, isn't it?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: It would be unusual to find clots. You quite often -- if the tubes have been in a long time, very often they get coated with just natural secretions from the lungs and because they're so small it doesn't take much to occlude the lumen with the secretions. But it would be unusual to have a tube blocked by a clot unless there was ongoing bleeding with -- as a consequence of low platelets or a clotting disorder or from a previous pulmonary haemorrhage. You wouldn't normally find blood in the trachea.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: But as it happens with [Baby G] on this occasion, the fact is, as recorded here, the end was blocked by an old clot, wasn't it?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes. That's what it says, yes.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: But her sats improved with bagging, so that's with the Neopuff and bagging?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes, because they'd taken the ET tube out so it had to be with a Neopuff.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: Right. Will that be, from what you can see here, because air wasn't going through the ET tube because of the clot, so once it was taken out and she was given oxygen with the Neopuff and bagging, she did improve?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes. She desaturated because the ventilator was unable to push gas into her lungs because of the clot or secretions, a mixture of both, at the end of that tube.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: So if you're not ventilating then you will desaturate.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: So that's a very sudden thing. That's a very sudden event.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: "Fairly stable day. Ventilation unchanged. Has had several desaturations without bradycardia requiring oxygen. Large oral secretions. Small to moderate ET secretions. Slight pink bloodstained secretions at last suction."

blocks.text: Yes.

blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: I wasn't suggesting that.
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: No, no, you asked if there were other causes and that's a natural cause where you can get pink-stained secretions.

blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: Next, please, 29 June, so about a month now into [Baby G]'s life, page 4314, Mr Murphy. It's the bottom half of that page. I might need your assistance here with interpreting some of this, Dr Bohin. An entry at 4.20 in the morning.
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: "Asked to review by staff nurse. Desaturation.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: Increased oxygen [something] 23 plus 6. Now day 30.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: The corrected gestation is therefore 28 weeks [that's 28/40]. Bradycardia to 65 beats per minute. Problems: prematurity (inaudible) RDS. On DART."

blocks.text: "Hypophosphataemia [so her was phosphate low].
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: Thrombocytopaenia [which means her platelets are low].
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: PDA..."
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: Which is a patent ductus arteriosus, which is an additional blood vessel that babies have when they're inside their mum's womb, that usually would close in a few days after birth, but in premature babies quite often stays open.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: We see she's on the ventilator, is that?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes. She is on SIMV ventilation, so synchronised intermittent mandatory ventilation, so is not on the oscillator
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: anymore. And it gives you the ventilatory pressures, which are moderate.

blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: It's standard. I would call that standard ventilation.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: "Saturations down to 50%."
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: "Down to 50%. Required oxygen increased to 80%."
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: She was in 60% oxygen before and in order to treat her desaturation she required the oxygen to go up to 80%.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: And then the examination?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: "Decreased air entry right base."
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: I don't know if that says -- yes:
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: "Squeaky auscultation on the left. Staff nurse suctioned. Fresh blood on suction tube. Looking pale.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: Heart sounds, number 1, number 2."
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: And she's got a loud murmur which would be consistent with the PDA, which is item number 5 on the sheet:
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: "Chest X-ray requested. Contacted the specialist registrar. Will come to review. Pressure on ventilator increased to 18/5 from 18/4."
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: So just looking at that, we have desaturation down to 50%, albeit on a less invasive form of ventilation at this time, don't we?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes.

blocks.text: "05.16. Bleeped at the time of event but busy on paediatric ward. History and events noted. Fresh blood in ET on suction. Significant desat prior to this requiring 50..."

blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: "Chest X-ray..."
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Then it says:
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: "Diagnosis: probable pulmonary haemorrhage."
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: "Attempt venous access and coag. Vitamin K. If cannot get another cannula, give oral. Keep PEEP at 6."
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: And an ultrasound of the head.

blocks.text: And it continues here at 5.50 on the daily review.
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: I just want to go to where it says "problems" if we could:
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: "Prematurity. Probable pulmonary haemorrhage.
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Hypoglycaemia. PDA. Hypophosphataemia."
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: We had seen at the page before "diagnosis: probable pulmonary haemorrhage" and it says "probable pulmonary haemorrhage" here. That's, first of all, because we're dealing with fresh blood rather than something mixed in with a secretion, isn't it?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes. And it's in -- on the previous problem list, which is omitted from this list, it says thrombocytopaenia, which is low platelet count, which would predispose you to bleeding spontaneously.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: But just pausing there, yesterday Dr Evans said that pulmonary haemorrhage is a killer. And I took issue with that. Pulmonary haemorrhage is not necessarily a killer, is it?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: In the majority of times it is, certainly in a baby this fragile, because with a pulmonary haemorrhage, rather than just having less than a millilitre of bloodstained secretions or a small amount of bloodstained secretions, with a frank pulmonary haemorrhage you normally got lots and lots of fresh blood coming up the trachea, such that you cannot suck it out quick enough, and it's that that means that you cannot resuscitate these babies. So if this was a pulmonary haemorrhage, and I don't know that it was, in the face of low platelet count it was certainly very mild.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: Yes. It doesn't appear that anybody, as we can see from the notes, is reacting to it as if it's about a killer, does it?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: No, but she's already seriously ill at this point.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: But it simply isn't right to say that a pulmonary haemorrhage is inevitably a killer, is it?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: It's not inevitable but in a baby of this size and gestation, it --
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: And we see --
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: In a baby of this size and gestation?
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: It would usually be if it was a frank pulmonary haemorrhage.

blocks.speaker: MR MYERS

blocks.text: Yes.

blocks.text: -- not because of suction, but bleeding for whatever reason?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: Sorry:

blocks.text: months old. So at this point [Baby G] is still or is marked as desaturating, isn't she?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes, I think I read that when I was speaking to Mr Johnson as she was having self-correcting desaturations and, over the course of a whole night shift, she appears to have had three over the course of a whole night shift and I also mention that the 10ml aspirate, but that was the only large aspirate during that time.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: Yes, all right. There was an aspirate and it appears that her stomach had distended after the feed, is that correct, because it says:
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: "Abdomen 30 centimetres, usually 26 to 27"?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: With all respect to [Baby G]'s mum, this was measured by her mother, and I would -- it depends on where you measure the abdomen from, whether you measure at the same point each time. So I'm not sure if that's an accurate reflection. It may represent a distension.

blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes. That's highlighted, I think.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: Ah, thank you.

blocks.text: We know that [Baby G] was discharged from Arrowe Park Hospital on 13 August and went to the Countess of Chester then. But that wasn't the first time that attempts had been made for her to be transferred to the Countess of Chester, was it?
blocks.speaker: MR MYERS

blocks.text: No.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: On this occasion here we have, 31 July 2015:
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: "[Baby G] transferred to transport incubator..."
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Pausing there, that's a particular incubator designed to do what it says, assist in transporting a baby from one establishment to another?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: That's correct, yes.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: So transferred to the transport incubator:
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Is that capillary blood gas taken?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: And satisfactory:
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: "Handover given. [Baby G] then started to desaturate to 42% with associated bradycardia to 70s."

blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: "Neopuffing required. Decision made by consultants not to transfer to Chester. [Baby G] now back in incubator, parents aware."

blocks.text: So what happened there was [Baby G] was due to be transported and then, for whatever reason, there's a significant but profound desaturation to 42%, and her heart rate drops, and the decision was taken that it wasn't the right time to transfer her to Chester; is that correct?

blocks.text: That's correct but she must have recovered because they immunised her the next day, so she must have recovered from that.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Transporting babies from one hospital to another is fraught with difficulty and babies do not travel well and sick babies do not travel well. So I think that was a wise decision. If the baby had desaturated in that way on transfer -- by the mere action of transferring from one incubator to another, the baby was unlikely to travel well that day, so that was the right decision, not to transfer her.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: Pausing there, we have seen already in the last entry that at about 6 o'clock in the morning on the same day there had been the three desaturations observed around about the time of the feed.
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Well, she was having self-limiting desaturations with feeds all along. That's quite a normal occurrence. If they're self-limiting and babies correct themselves, that's not a problem.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: The three desaturations happened over the course of the whole night, they weren't all altogether in one batch, they were over a long period.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: She displayed a tendency to desaturate, didn't she?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: She had desaturations associated with feed, which is absolutely standard for a baby of that gestation and age.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: And then at 17.40 she had quite a profound desaturation —
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes, she did.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: -- when she was due to be transported?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes.

blocks.text: Now, we are compelled to observe that wasn't relevant and it's something which in fact is potentially prejudicial depending on the way this goes. blocks.speaker: MR MYERS

blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Okay. You'd certainly noticed it was attached when you'd been going backwards and forwards behind -- when the doctors were there.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: NURSE B: Yes.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Is there any reason why -- well, let's concentrate on what you can remember first, okay? Tell us what Lucy was doing. Did she tell you anything?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: NURSE B: She said that [Baby G] wasn't breathing and I could clearly see she wasn't. She didn't look well at all.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: And what did you see yourself of [Baby G], as you could see [Baby G]?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: NURSE B: I could see she wasn't breathing and she was a poor colour. She wasn't moving.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: What do you mean by poor colour?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: NURSE B: Well, she already looked pale.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: NURSE B: But she was -- I don't remember, I just remember she just did not look well. What specific colour, I don't know.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Okay. Do you remember making a statement during the course of this investigation?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: NURSE B: Yes.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: And have you refreshed your memory from the statement today?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: NURSE B: Yes.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Do you remember whether -- were things at least fresher in your mind at the time you made the statement than they are now? I know the statement wasn't made until 2 March 2018, so it was --
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: NURSE B: In terms of the colour, I don't remember.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Okay. In terms of the alarm and whether it was attached?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: NURSE B: I don't remember if it was attached. The monitor wasn't on.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: The monitor wasn't on?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: NURSE B: No. I don't remember if it was attached but the monitor wasn't -- the actual physical screen was off.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Right, okay. So going back to what you told us before about alarms and silencing alarms and the ability to actually switch the monitor off, it had been switched off?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: NURSE B: Yes.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: On those occasions when you'd gone behind the curtain and you'd seen -- you recall seeing it attached to the baby, albeit in different places, was it switched on on those occasions?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: NURSE B: It was, yes.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Do you recall how Lucy seemed when you saw her behind the screen assisting [Baby G]?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: NURSE B: She obviously was concerned --
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: NURSE B: -- and she was responding appropriately.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Right. Now, you weren't in a position to help at that stage, so I think you shouted for Caroline Bennion; is that right?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: NURSE B: That's correct.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: And I think Caroline came very quickly and assisted Lucy Letby?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: NURSE B: She did.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Do you recall the two doctors coming back?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: NURSE B: No, I'd excused myself.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Okay. All right. Was [Baby G] then -- did [Baby G] respond to the treatment that she was given?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: NURSE B: Yes, very quickly.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: And having responded to the treatment, was she at least at that stage stabilised in the unit?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: NURSE B: She was moved to nursery 1 --
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Right.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: NURSE B: -- went on to Optiflow, put on to the full monitoring, and under very close observation.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Did you continue care for [Baby G] once she was moved into room 1?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: NURSE B: Yes.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Okay. Was [Baby G]'s mum informed of what had happened?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: NURSE B: She was informed of [Baby G] stopping breathing, yes.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Did she come back to the unit?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: NURSE B: She was already on the unit. She was in the family room. She came of course, yes, immediately.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Once [Baby G] was moved to room 1, I think -- was she placed in an incubator at this point?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: NURSE B: She was, yes.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: And was she placed in an incubator now without clothes, so her colour could be, as it were, monitored more closely?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: NURSE B: Yes.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: I think you mentioned that she was put on Optiflow at that stage.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: NURSE B: Yes.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Do you remember anything about [Baby G]'s tummy when she was moved to number 1?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: NURSE B: According to my statement I've said her tummy was normal. Her poos were abnormal, but her tummy was normal.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Thank you. And did you continue to care for [Baby G] for the rest of the shift on a one-to-one basis?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: NURSE B: I don't remember.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Okay. All right. Perhaps if we can look at initially tile 78, please, Mr Murphy.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: That, as it were, is the continuing observation chart from 4 o'clock. I wonder if we could go to tile 83, please. We probably don't need to look at that again, I apologise. If we go to tile 83. We can have a look at that, please.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY
